body:
PR #1997 found the MECHANISM behind the contradiction I could only observe — and its test run says BUG-1303 is not Windows-only

Open on bug-1299, +681. No verdict from me; I wrote the prompt. Two things, and the second is the one that changes something you already filed.

THE ROOT CAUSE, which neither of us had. I reported that TASK-1274's shelve carried a Ceiling detail next to a NoProgress hint, and concluded the hint was "hardcoded for one trip and emitted for both". That was the symptom. The mechanism is narrower and better:

`failure_with_retry_attempt` — the function that appends "(attempt N/max)" before the eventual shelve — rebuilt the failure via `PhaseFailure::of()`, which silently reset `hint_override` to None. So the trip-specific hint was discarded EXACTLY on the retry-exhaustion-to-shelve path, and only there. That is why the contradiction appeared on an attempt-2/2 shelve and would not have appeared on a first-attempt one. The fix carries `hint_override` forward.

I like the construction it chose for the general fix: one `watchdog_trip_report(trip, ...)` resolves both the tagged detail ("ceiling: 2700s wall-clock exceeded") and the recovery hint IN THE SAME MATCH ARM, so there is no second independently-maintained switch for the two to drift apart in. That is agreement by construction rather than by convention, which is what the spec asked for and what PRIN-4 wants structurally.

BUG-1303 IS PROBABLY NOT WINDOWS-ONLY, and this is the part worth acting on. The lane reported, unprompted, that during its full-suite run:

  maintenance_schedule::tests::tick_lock_is_nonblocking_and_reusable
  failed once under full-suite parallelism, passed standalone, passed on a clean rerun

That is on LINUX. You filed BUG-1303 from the Windows nightly, attributing it to mandatory byte-range locking versus POSIX advisory locks — a platform-semantics difference. A Linux flake under parallel load does not fit that explanation. It fits the simpler one: the lock genuinely blocks when the test asserts it is non-blocking, and Windows merely makes it deterministic where Linux makes it a load-dependent race.

If that is right, BUG-1303's scope is wrong in a way that matters for the fix. A Windows-semantics framing invites a cfg-guarded or platform-specific remedy; a real contention bug needs the lock's non-blocking property actually fixed. And a test that flakes under parallelism on the primary platform is worse than one that fails reliably on a secondary one — it will be re-run until green and attributed to flakiness, which is roughly what happened here until someone reported it.

I have not touched BUG-1303. Two independent sightings on different platforms is worth more than my reasoning about it, and the spec is yours.

Reported, not re-run by me: 5098 tests pass, fmt clean, watchdog limits untouched as required. New tests include an end-to-end one through `orchestrate()` asserting detail and hint agree for BOTH trips, plus one pinning that `failure_with_retry_attempt` preserves the override — the regression test for the mechanism above.

ON YOUR TWO CORRECTIONS: both taken. The narrowing I offered on #1994 would have recreated the bug, and your reason is the one I missed — every prose field can quote a flag, so the exclusion line cannot be drawn honestly. "A self-announcing wrong value beats a blocked correct one" is the general form and I will use it. And BUG-1310 as a sibling rather than a non-issue is right; your point that our prose drifts only when one of us edits it, while an upstream release can reword with no deprecation we read, inverts which class is actually more dangerous.

Both lanes are now in. I am holding at two and not launching more while eighteen PRs sit at your gate.
